Research life / Personal reflections

Finding a Postdoctoral Position

By Rohit Shrivastava · 7 min read

Taking a postdoctoral position is a major career decision. You will find articles explaining why a postdoc is worthwhile and others arguing that it can be bad for your career. There is no single answer that applies to everyone. The question to ask yourself is: how will a postdoc help me achieve my career goals? For me, a good postdoctoral position can be the icing on the cake. But that may not be true for you.

Why do a postdoc?

Because you are fascinated by the research. I feel that you should do a postdoc if you have a strong desire to investigate a particular topic and the lab or principal investigator (PI) you have chosen motivates you to pursue your research goals. A postdoc can help you learn advanced techniques, deepen your knowledge, and contribute to society. For many researchers, doing research is their way of making the world a better place. For others, finding a solution to a real-world problem is immensely rewarding.

Because you want a career in research. If you want to work in academic or industrial research, a postdoc may help you gain skills and broaden your knowledge. However, it is not essential for every research role, especially outside academia. You may also hear concerns that moving into industry becomes harder after a postdoc. It is worth speaking to people in the roles you want before deciding whether further academic training will help you get there.

Who should you ask for advice?

Your PhD supervisor. Your supervisor knows your scientific abilities and can be a useful starting point. But a great scientist is not necessarily a good career adviser. Some supervisors may recommend a postdoc by default, even if your interests and skills would also suit a career in industry.

Your friends and lab mates. Many of us take our own abilities for granted. A friend or colleague may recognise strengths that you have overlooked, and those strengths could matter in either academia or industry.

Postdocs in your own and other labs. Ask about their experiences, what they have gained, and what they wish they had known before starting.

Your university’s careers service. I strongly recommend this. Careers advisers can help you explore opportunities inside and outside academia. They may also be able to point you towards funding opportunities if you want to apply for your own fellowship.

Other academic staff. Members of your PhD committee and recently appointed PIs can offer useful perspectives, particularly on the transition to an independent career.

Yourself. Listen to what you want. Do not do a postdoc simply because everyone else in your lab has done one, and do not treat it as the default next step. Whatever you choose should be something you can enjoy and should help you develop. By the end of a postdoc, you should be able to explain clearly what you can offer a future employer.

How do you apply for a postdoctoral position?

During your PhD, you will probably have identified the areas of research that interest you most. A postdoc can be an opportunity to cross disciplinary boundaries and gain new skills and knowledge. Think about how those skills fit the career you want.

You can look for advertised positions on sites such as EURAXESS, Nature Careers, Science Careers, PostdocJobs, and EuroScienceJobs. You can also approach researchers you have met at conferences. If a talk or a conversation sparked your interest in their work, mention it. Be specific and explain why you would like to work with them.

A position in a famous lab may sound attractive, but reputation is not everything. Choose a lab where you can fit in, learn, and contribute, with room for a two-way exchange of knowledge.

I suggest applying to a small number of labs with a concrete research idea that connects to their work. An original idea can leave a lasting impression. It shows that you have read their papers, thought about their research, and can develop ideas of your own. Technical skills can be taught, but learning to formulate a useful research question takes time.

I have seen people send the same template email to researchers around the world without reading their research profiles, sometimes without even changing the name in the cover letter. That can undermine an application before the PI has looked at the applicant’s experience.

Keep your initial email brief, ideally around five or six lines. Tailor your CV and cover letter to explain both what you can contribute and how the position would help you develop. Put the details of your achievements in those documents rather than repeating them all in the email. You can also include links to your ORCID, Google Scholar, or LinkedIn profile.

Avoid filling the email with general praise. If you admire someone’s work, explain the specific connection to your own interests or ideas. Focus on how your experience could help address a research question and what you hope to learn. A thoughtful application gives a PI something concrete to respond to, although even a strong application may not receive a reply.

Personally, I wanted to move beyond the exact field of my PhD. I felt that working on a different problem would help me learn more and bring something new to the host lab. That does not mean staying in the same field is always a mistake. What matters is whether the position offers room to grow.

It is also worth considering an independent fellowship rather than relying only on a PI’s existing funding. Examples of programmes to investigate include Newton fellowships in the UK, Alexander von Humboldt fellowships in Germany, JSPS fellowships in Japan, Marie Skłodowska-Curie fellowships in Europe, Human Frontier Science Program fellowships, and Banting fellowships in Canada. Programme names, availability, and eligibility can change, so check the relevant funder’s information before applying. There are also many country-specific schemes. This collection of postdoctoral funding schemes can be a starting point.

Writing a fellowship application helps you understand the proposed project, develop your writing, and think about budgets and research planning. Securing your own funding can also strengthen an application for a future faculty position.

In the search for a postdoc, do not lose sight of what makes you different. Keep looking for opportunities to learn and step outside your comfort zone.

Your PhD supervisor may be able to introduce you to collaborators. This can be a useful route into a position, but I would still ask whether the role would broaden your skills and knowledge. A familiar connection should not be the only reason to choose a lab.

What should you gain from good postdoctoral training?

Whether you work in academia or industry, the right host lab, PI, and institution should help you develop in several ways.

New research skills. Each position should give you opportunities to learn techniques and expand your knowledge. Working across disciplines or sectors can broaden your career options and show that you can learn beyond your original area of expertise. For example, combining experimental work with programming for data analysis can be a useful strength.

Transferable skills. Postdoctoral training should involve more than producing good science. You should also have opportunities to communicate your work, supervise students, and help manage research. This might include conference presentations, papers, fellowship and grant applications, teaching, and public engagement through talks or open days.

Working well with others. Scientific training alone does not prepare someone to lead a group. Understanding gender equality and learning to work respectfully with colleagues from different cultural and religious backgrounds are also important.

Management skills. Researchers spend years learning how to do science, but becoming a group leader also means becoming a manager. Many have little formal preparation for that change. A postdoc can be a good time to learn about project planning, budgets, and managing research activities.

Support towards an independent career. Keep your career goals in mind and discuss them with your PI or another mentor. Together, identify the skills you still need and make a career development plan. If you want to become a group leader, this could include developing a research programme, writing grants, managing projects, preparing your CV, and practising for interviews.

Entrepreneurship and networking. If you want to move into industry, look for opportunities to learn about commercialisation and intellectual property. Attend events that bring academic and industrial researchers together. Some institutes also offer courses in intellectual property and entrepreneurship.
